# Markov Chains

:::{#exr-04-LA-cars}
Suppose that we work for a car rental company that has two
locations, $P$ and $Q$.  When a customer rents a car
at one location, they have the option to return it to either
location at the end of the day.  After doing some market
research, we determine:

* 80% of the cars rented at location $P$ are
	returned to $P$ and 20% are returned to
	$Q$. 

* 60% of the cars rented at location $Q$ are
	returned to $Q$ and 40% are returned to
	$P$. 
	
a. Suppose that there are 1000 cars at location $P$
and no cars at location $Q$ on Monday morning.  How many
cars are there at locations $P$ and $Q$ at the end
of the day on Monday?

b. How many are at locations $P$ and $Q$ at end
of the day on Tuesday? 

c. Let $P_t$ and $Q_t$ be the number of
	cars at locations $P$ and $Q$, respectively, at the
	end of day $t$. Write a system of equations 
	that shows how to compute $P_{t+1}$  and $Q_{t+1}$ 
	from $P_t$ and $Q_t$.

e. Use your matrix-vector equation and Python to compute the number of cars at each
location each day for a week.

f. Write a matrix-vector equation that can be used to compute the number of cars
at each location after 8 days (next Monday night). 
What is the matrix in this equation? 
How can you compute it in Python?^[Note: You may find `np.matrix_power()` to be a useful
function.]

g. Write a for loop to display $\xvec_1, \xvec_2, \xvec_3, \dots \xvec_{50}$.
What do you notice about this sequence?

:::{#exr-04-LA-cars-probs}

In @exr-04-LA-cars, we worked with the *number* of cars at each location.

a. Re-express this in terms of the *proportion* of cars at each location.
That is, find the matrix $B$ such that 
$$
\yvec_{t+1} = B \yvec_t
$$
where the elements of $\yvec$ are the proportions of cars at locations $P$ and $Q$. 

b. How does the matrix $B$ compare to the matrix you found in @exr-04-LA-cars?

\vfill
:::


The sequence of probability vectors that we obtain by a process like this is called 
a **Markov chain**.

{{< pagebreak >}}

:::{#exr-moving-people}
Here's an (oversimplified) example involving people rather than cars.
Every year, people move between urban (U), suburban (S), and rural (R) populations with
probabilities given in the figure below.

![Movement of people between Urban, Suburban, and Rural.](../images/stoch-pops.pdf)


*Note: This exercise is related to [Exercise 5.5.5.2](https://ula-ds.netlify.app/sec-stochastic#exercise-186) from ULA-DS, and there 
is a python cell there that you may find handy for parts of this.*


a. Construct a matrix $A$ so that the matrix equation $\xvec_{t+1} = A \xvec_{t}$ describes
the movement of the cars (in proportions, no counts).

b. Say in words what $A_{ij}$ tells you about this situation.
That is, what number goes in row $i$, coluns $j$ of the matrix $A$?

c. The columns of matrices $A$ and $B$ (from the previous exercise) 
have a special property. 
What is it? Why must they have this property? (Such matrices are called 
**stochastic matrices**.)

d. Each of the vectors in a Markov chain also have a special property? What is it?
(Such vectors are called **probability vectors**.)

e. Compute several iterations of the Markov chain.  Does it appear to be converging?
If so, to what vector? Let's call that vector $\qvec$.

f. Compute $C \qvec$. What interesting thing happens? 

    (This is a general feature of converging Markov chains. 
The vector $\qvec$ is called a **steady state vector** and is a special example.)
:::

If we have a matrix $A$, a vector $\vvec$, and a scalar $\lambda$ such that
$$
A \vvec = \lambda \vvec
$$
then $\vvec$ is called an **eigenvector** for $A$ and $\lambda$ is called an
**eigenvalue**.  Since they come together as a pair, they are often referred to
as an **eigenpair**.  Notice that multiplying a matrix by an eignevector is especially 
easy/efficient since we can replace matrix multiplication with scalar multiplication.

Since matrix multiplication forms a linear transformation, if we can write a vector
as a linear combination of eigenvectors, then we can use scalar multiplication for that
too.

:::{#exr-eigen-linear-combo}
Suppose we have eigenpairs $\twovec 21, 10$ and $\twovec{-1}2, -5$ for a matrix $A$.
Compute the following.

$A \twovec 21$, \quad
$A \twovec {-1}2$, \quad
$A \twovec {1}3$, \quad
$A \twovec {0}5$, \quad
$A \twovec {0}1$, \quad
$A \twovec {1}0$


What is the matrix $A$?
:::

If you have had some linear algebra before, you probably have learned a method for 
finding eigenvalues.^[The method usually taught in an introductory course involves 
computing the determinant of the matrix $A - \lambda I$, but you don't need to know about
that or about determinants for this course.]  That method can exhibit unfortunate numerical behavior, so the usual computational method for computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors
is based on the **power method**, which involves a clever use of repeated multiplication
with the matrix, much like we did with our Markov chain above.

Numpy can use this method to compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors using `numpy.linalg.eig()`.^[If you are interested, you can learn more about the power method
in [*ULA:DS*, Section 5.6: Finding eigenvectors numerically](https://ula-ds.netlify.app/sec-power-method.html#sec-power-method).]

:::{#exr-eig}
Use `np.linal.eig()` to compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix from
@exr-moving-people.  How do those results compare to your solution above? Why is the eigenvalue what it is?
:::

___

Not all Markov chains converge, but there is a condition that guarantees 
convergence: If 

* the stochastic matrix is positive (all the values of $A$ or of some power $A^t$ are positive), 
* 1 is an eigenvalue, and
* all the other eigenvalues have absolute value less than 1.

then the Markov chain converges to the eigenvector associated with eigenvalue 
$\lambda = 1$. (See [Theorem 5.5.6: Perron-Frobenius](https://ula-ds.netlify.app/sec-stochastic#theorem-perron).)

:::{#exr-chutes-ladders}
### Chutes and Ladders
Chutes and Ladders is an old children's game.
Exercise 10 at <https://ula-ds.netlify.app/sec-stochastic#exercise-194>
has you analyze a simplified version of this game as a Markov chain.  There 
are some nice diagrams and also some helpful Python chunks there.
Work through this problem.

**BONUS:**
Want a bit of a coding challenge? Try analyzing the full Chutes and Ladders game.
The only tricky part is defining the larger ($100 \times 100$) matrix involved.
Some helpful hints:

* It can be handy to create this matrix as the product of two matrices. The first deals with
the dice roles and ignores the chutes and ladders.  The second deals with the chutes and ladders.

* Be careful about the "edge conditions".  For example, when you roll the dice, you have an equal chance of landing on a square 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 squares away -- unless you are on one of the last few squares. Any time you roll a number that sould send you "off the board", you stop on the last square.  Taking this into account requires a little extra effort.

* Make sure you get things in the correct row and column. 
(What property should the columns of your stochastic matrix have? You can check this using
`A.sum(axis = ...)` if `A` is your matrix.)
:::
